problem: The bullet 'If one rule is needed in two places, add a new start symbol and keep the old variable for the inner use' does not belong to this conversion and can mislead. In the layered grammar the variable E is used in two places (as the start symbol and inside F → ( E )) and no new start symbol is added. A student may think the grammar shown is incomplete.
fix: Replace with: 'A variable can be used in more than one rule. Here E is both the start symbol and the variable inside F → ( E ), which is allowed.'

problem: The line 'Some syllabi call this conversion ambiguous CFG to unambiguous CFG' can be read as a general method. In general no method exists that turns an arbitrary ambiguous CFG into an unambiguous one; the layering only works because of operator precedence in expression grammars.
fix: Say: 'Some syllabi call this layering "ambiguous CFG to unambiguous CFG". It works only for expression grammars of this shape; in general there is no method to remove ambiguity from a grammar (Section 3).'

problem: The caption says the two groupings give 7 and 9, but neither the caption nor the figure states the id values, so a reader has no way to check these numbers from the figure alone.
fix: Add the values to the caption: '... with id₁ = 1, id₂ = 2, id₃ = 3 the plus-at-root grouping gives 1 + 2 × 3 = 7 and the times-at-root grouping gives (1 + 2) × 3 = 9.'

problem: The clause after the second language is tagged 'where:' but it explains instead of defining symbols, and it writes 'when n = m' while n and m already have fixed roles in the two parts. The reader must work out which n and m are being compared.
fix: Write: 'Here n and m are non-negative integers. Both parts contain aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ at n = m, and this shared set forces every grammar for the language to be ambiguous.'

problem: 'Fix the given grammar and test again' suggests that testing a grammar for ambiguity is always possible, which contradicts Q7 and Section 3 (it is undecidable).
fix: 'No. You must show that every grammar for L is ambiguous. One unambiguous grammar for L is enough to show L is not inherently ambiguous.'

problem: Shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts are LR-parser (yacc/bison) terms. ANTLR is not an LR parser and reports ambiguity or alternative-matching warnings, not shift/reduce conflicts.
fix: 'Parser generators such as yacc and bison report shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflicts that often come from ambiguous rules; ANTLR warns when two alternatives can match the same input. GLR parsers accept ambiguous grammars and return several trees.'

problem: '(see 3.6)' and 'Unit 6 covers that result' are plain text, so on a phone the student cannot jump to those units.
fix: Make them chapter links, e.g. 3.6 and Unit 6.
